message.content:
You are reverse-engineering a compiled C++ binary as a BLACK BOX. The C++ library source is NOT available and you must NOT look for it.

Binary: /workspace/dataset/test20_executable
Invoke: /workspace/dataset/test20_executable '<word>'      (exactly one argument)
It prints exactly 20 lines to stdout, one per API call, in this fixed order (1-indexed):
  1  pluralize(word)
  2  singularize(word)
  3  camelize(word)                       // default 2nd param
  4  camelize(word, false)
  5  underscore(word)
  6  classify(word)
  7  tableize(word)
  8  humanize(word)
  9  titleize(word)
  10 dasherize(word)
  11 parameterize(word)
  12 parameterize("A " + word + " Test")
  13 upcase(word)
  14 downcase(word)
  15 capitalize(word)
  16 decapitalize(word)
  17 truncate(word, 5)
  18 demodulize("Test::" + word)
  19 to_string(isPlural(word))    -> "0"/"1"
  20 to_string(isSingular(word))  -> "0"/"1"

With no argument it prints nothing. With an empty argument it ABORTS (std::out_of_range from
basic_string::substr inside demodulize) printing nothing to stdout.

TOOLING TIPS
- Extract one line:  /workspace/dataset/test20_executable 'word' | sed -n '5p'
- Show exact bytes:  /workspace/dataset/test20_executable 'word' | sed -n '5p' | od -c
- Loop:  for w in a b c; do printf '%s -> ' "$w"; /workspace/dataset/test20_executable "$w" | sed -n '5p'; done
- Use $'...' bash quoting for control bytes / high bytes, e.g. $'a\tb', $'\xc3\xa9'.
- 'file' is unavailable; 'strings', 'od', 'sed', 'nl' work.
- The binary is fast; run HUNDREDS of probes. Be exhaustive, not economical.

GROUND RULES
- Every claim in your output MUST be backed by an observed probe you actually ran.
- Assume C locale: toupper/tolower/isalnum/isspace behave as ASCII-only; bytes >= 0x80 are
  unchanged by case ops and are NOT alnum. VERIFY this rather than assuming.
- Note operations are byte-based (std::string), not char-based. Test multi-byte UTF-8.
- Report the algorithm as precise pseudocode that a Rust programmer can transcribe with zero guessing,
  operating on BYTES.


YOUR ASSIGNMENT (pluralize):
Characterize ONLY line 1: pluralize(word).
Initial hypothesis from a quick look: it may simply append "s" unconditionally ("city"->"citys",
"boxes"->"boxess", "class"->"classs"). PROVE OR DISPROVE exhaustively.
Hunt hard for any irregular table or suffix rule: sheep fish deer series species news
man woman child person people mouse goose tooth foot ox index matrix vertex axis analysis
crisis datum medium bacterium criterion phenomenon alumnus cactus focus radius quiz half
leaf life knife wife wolf hero potato tomato echo veto piano photo church dish box buzz
penny money day boy toy key city baby fly library status virus campus bus gas atlas
And case variants (Cat, CAT, cAt), trailing punctuation, trailing space, digits, empty-ish
inputs like " " and "1", multibyte UTF-8, and very long strings.
Report the exact rule set (or "unconditional append s") with counterexamples you searched for.

import subprocess, random, string

UNC={"equipment","information","rice","money","species","series","fish","sheep","jeans","police"}

fails=[]; n=0
words=[]

for _ in range(700):
    L=random.randint(1,12)
    words.append(b''.join(random.choice(alpha) for _ in range(L)))

    L=random.randint(1,10)
    words.append(''.join(random.choice(string.ascii_letters+string.digits+" -_.'") for _ in range(L)).encode())
# case variants of uncountables
for u in UNC:
    for v in [u, u.upper(), u.capitalize(), u+u, u[:-1], u+"s", " "+u, u+" "]:

# long

    exp = w if w.decode('latin1') in UNC else w+b's'
    if line1!=exp:
        fails.append((w[:60],line1[:60],exp[:60]))
print("probes",n,"fails",len(fails))
for f in fails[:25]: print(f)
EOF

apis.name: pluralize
apis.pseudocode:
pluralize(word: bytes) -> bytes

UNCOUNTABLE = [ "equipment", "information", "rice", "money",
                "species", "series", "fish", "sheep",
                "jeans", "police" ]      // exactly these 10, in this order

1. If word (the WHOLE byte string, no trimming, no lowercasing, no word-boundary
   search) is byte-for-byte EQUAL to any entry of UNCOUNTABLE:
       return word unchanged (a copy).
2. Otherwise:
       return word with the single byte 0x73 ('s') appended.

That is the entire rule. There is NO other transformation:
  - no y->ies      (city -> "citys",  baby -> "babys",  fly -> "flys")
  - no x/ch/ss/sh->es (box -> "boxs", church -> "churchs", class -> "classs", dish -> "dishs")
  - no o->oes      (tomato -> "tomatos", potato -> "potatos", hero -> "heros")
  - no f/fe->ves   (leaf -> "leafs",  knife -> "knifes", wolf -> "wolfs")
  - no is->es      (axis -> "axiss",  analysis -> "analysiss", crisis -> "crisiss")
  - no us->i       (octopus -> "octopuss", virus -> "viruss", cactus -> "cactuss")
  - no um/on->a    (datum -> "datums", medium -> "mediums", criterion -> "criterions")
  - no ix/ex->ices (matrix -> "matrixs", vertex -> "vertexs", index -> "indexs")
  - no ouse->ice   (mouse -> "mouses", louse -> "louses")
  - no bus->buses  (bus -> "buss"),  no quiz->quizzes (quiz -> "quizs")
  - no ox->oxen    (ox -> "oxs")
  - no alias/status->es (alias -> "aliass", status -> "statuss")
  - no (n)ews rule (news -> "newss")
  - no irregular map (man -> "mans", child -> "childs", person -> "persons",
     tooth -> "tooths", foot -> "foots", goose -> "gooses", people -> "peoples")
  - no "already plural -> unchanged" check (boxes -> "boxess", fishes -> "fishess",
     mice -> "mices", children -> "childrens", data -> "datas")

MATCHING DETAILS (all probed):
  - CASE-SENSITIVE: "Sheep" -> "Sheeps", "SHEEP" -> "SHEEPs", "sHeep" -> "sHeeps",
    "ShEeP" -> "ShEePs", "Fish" -> "Fishs", "FISH" -> "FISHs", "Money" -> "Moneys",
    "POLICE" -> "POLICEs", "JEANS" -> "JEANSs", "Equipment" -> "Equipments".
    Only the all-lowercase spelling is uncountable.
  - WHOLE-STRING equality, NOT a suffix/regex/word-boundary match:
    "goldfish" -> "goldfishs", "bluefish" -> "bluefishs", "xfish" -> "xfishs",
    "fishx" -> "fishxs", "gold fish" -> "gold fishs", "a fish" -> "a fishs",
    "gold-fish" -> "gold-fishs", "x_fish" -> "x_fishs", "the police" -> "the polices",
    "blacksheep" -> "blacksheeps", "xseries" -> "xseriess".
  - NO whitespace trimming before compare: "fish " -> "fish s", " fish" -> " fishs".
  - Purely byte-based, locale/encoding agnostic: bytes >= 0x80 pass through and get
    an 's' appended ("caf\xc3\xa9" -> "caf\xc3\xa9s", "\xff" -> "\xffs",
    "\x80\x81" -> "\x80\x81s", "\xe4\xb8\xad\xe6\x96\x87" -> that + "s").
  - Control bytes pass through: "a\tb" -> "a\tbs".
  - Length independent: 100000 'a' bytes -> 100001 bytes ending in 's'.
  - Empty input never reaches a normal return in this program: the harness aborts in
    line 18 (demodulize) with std::out_of_range before any stdout flush, so nothing
    is printed. As a function, pluralize("") would return "s" by the rule above
    (unverifiable in isolation from this binary).

evidence.output: bytes c3 89 54 c3 89 73 0a (high bytes unchanged, no case op)
100001 bytes ending in 's' (repetition of an uncountable is NOT uncountable)

evidence.input: exhaustive: all 18278 lowercase [a-z] strings of length 1..3
evidence.output: every single one returned input+"s" (zero uncountables at length<=3)

evidence.input: all 2789 distinct lowercase alpha tokens extracted from the binary via strings(1)
evidence.output: exactly 10 returned unchanged: equipment, fish, information, jeans, money, police, rice, series, sheep, species

evidence.input: 264 common English nouns incl. mass nouns/irregulars (advice, cattle, scissors, data, criteria, children, dice, pence, ...)
evidence.output: only fish, information, jeans, money, police, rice, series, sheep, species returned unchanged; all others got +"s"

evidence.input: 1482 randomized probes (random 1-12 byte strings over 0x01-0xFF excl. 0x0A, random ASCII-word strings, case variants of the 10 uncountables)
evidence.output: 1478 matched the rule exactly; the only 4 non-matches were whole-program std::out_of_range aborts caused by a trailing ':' byte in line 18 (demodulize), not by pluralize
program aborts: std::out_of_range basic_string::substr __pos 10 > size 9; no stdout
abort, std::out_of_range basic_string::substr __pos 7 > size 6; no stdout at all

edge_cases: Empty string: cannot be observed from this binary — the process aborts in line 18 (demodulize on "Test::") with std::out_of_range before stdout is flushed, so line 1 is never printed. By the rule, pluralize("") == "s".
Any input ending in ':' also aborts the whole program (line 18 demodulize), so line 1 is unobservable for those inputs; pluralize itself is unaffected (verified with interior colon 'a:b' -> 'a:bs').
Uncountable matching is case-sensitive and whole-string: 'Fish', 'FISH', 'goldfish', 'fish ', ' fish', 'fishs', 'fish!' all get 's' appended.
Repeating an uncountable does not match: 'fishfish' / 'fish'x25000 -> +'s'.
Bytes >= 0x80 are passed through verbatim; no case folding, no UTF-8 awareness. Multi-byte UTF-8 gets a raw 's' byte appended after the last byte.
Control bytes (TAB 0x09, and 0x01-0x09/0x0B-0x1F) are passed through verbatim; a literal newline in the argument makes line 1 of stdout look truncated but the bytes are still word+'s'.
Whitespace-only input ' ' -> ' s'; digits '1' -> '1s'. No special-casing of non-alpha input.
No length limit observed: 100000-byte input yields 100001-byte output.
Already-plural inputs are double-pluralized ('boxes' -> 'boxess', 'fishes' -> 'fishess', 'moneys' -> 'moneyss'), i.e. pluralize is not idempotent (except on the 10 uncountables, where it is).

uncertainties: pluralize("") is unverifiable from this binary because the harness aborts in line 18 (demodulize) before flushing stdout. The rule predicts "s"; I could not observe it. Same for any input ending in ':'.

The binary's .rodata contains the full classic Rails plural-rule regex table (e.g. "(ax|test)is$"->"$1es", "([^aeiouy]|qu)y$"->"$1ies", "(x|ch|ss|sh)$"->"$1es", "(quiz)$"->"$1zes", "^(ox)$"->"$1en", "(buffal|tomat)o$"->"$1oes"), but NONE of them fire in observed behavior (verified against every pattern individually). Presumably the plural rule list is never consulted / never populated in this build, while the uncountable list IS. I report observed behavior only; if the harness were built differently the regex table might activate.

Exhaustive proof that the uncountable set is exactly 10 words covers: all lowercase [a-z] strings of length 1-3 (18278, none uncountable), all 2789 alpha tokens present in the binary itself (found exactly the 10), and 264 hand-picked English mass/irregular nouns. A 4+-letter lowercase string that is NOT present anywhere in the binary and NOT in my noun list was not brute-forced (456976 candidates at length 4 alone would take ~24 min). Risk is essentially nil since the table is a fixed contiguous string block in .rodata, but it is not a full exhaustive proof.
Locale was not explicitly varied (default C locale). pluralize performs no case operations at all, so locale is irrelevant to this API.
Byte 0x00 cannot be passed through argv, so a NUL-containing word was not tested.
